newsitem.title: CHINA: China intensifies battle against corruption.
newsitem.headline: China intensifies battle against corruption.

text.p: China's Communist Party has intensified its battle against corruption by banning senior officials from seeking profits for themselves, their friends, families and staff, the People's Daily said on Thursday.

The party issued a code of conduct recently, banning officials from personally engaging in profit-seeking activities and using their positions or influence to rake in illicit profits, the newspaper said.
The code of conduct also bans officials from seeking gains for friends, relatives and staff, and prohibits squandering public funds, extravagance and waste, it said.

It bans spouses and children of Communist Party members holding the rank of or above provincial governor or minister from running private businesses or working at wholly foreign-owned firms in the region under the jurisdiction of the official.
"This is...a major event in the building of a clean and honest government," said a commentary in the People's Daily, the party mouthpiece.

Corruption, virtually unknown in China in the years after the puritan communists toppled the corruption-riddled Nationalists and swept to power in 1949, has made a rapid and dramatic comeback in nearly two decades of market reform.
China's leaders have warned that corruption is a virus that could topple the party.
Chen Xitong became the most senior official to be ensnared in a corruption scandal since 1949 when he was sacked from the Communist Party's Politburo in September 1995.
He had already resigned as Beijing's Communist Party boss in April 1995 after his protege, Vice-Mayor Wang Baosen, committed suicide after coming under investigation for corruption.

Chen has not been seen in public for two years. Hong Kong's China-watching newspapers say Chen is under house arrest in Inner Mongolia after losing out in a power struggle to China's Communist Party chief and state president, Jiang Zemin.
One of Chen's sons has been detained and his mistress remains on the run.

In the booming southern city of Shenzhen, senior officials have been ordered to declare their annual income, financial situation and gifts from April in a bid to stamp out corruption, Hong Kong's Apple Daily said on Thursday.
About 500 officials in Shenzhen, just across the border from the British colony of Hong Kong, would be affected under the directive, the newspaper said.
Last week, the Communist Party's Discipline Inspection Commission issued the most detailed regulations in nearly a decade to tighten discipline.

The regulations bar party members from organising or joining groups, meetings or demonstrations opposed to the party line. Publication of writings or statements that challenge the leadership of the Communist Party is also prohibited.

The rules also tackle a rapidly spreading vice within party ranks -- womanising. They ban party members from visiting prostitutes, from acting as pimps, from receiving a massage from a member of the opposite sex and from seeing pornographic movies and publications.

The late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's open-door policy opened up loopholes for authorities to exploit their positions for personal gain while providing opportunities for officials to see pornography and visit prostitutes -- both eradicated in the early years of communist rule.
